result: Genetically diverse UPEC strains share a common transcriptional program during human UTI. The core genome showed high gene expression correlation across all 14 patient samples (median 0.91), which was distinct from in vitro urine cultures (median 0.73 correlation between patient and urine samples). PCA analysis confirmed patient samples form a tight cluster separate from in vitro cultures.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states this is 'the important discovery that reprogramming occurs' and 'a major strength of this work.' Reviewer 2 describes the authors as identifying 'a conserved expression pattern shared among all isolates.' No reviewers challenge this core finding about the common transcriptional program.

result: UPEC during infection show marked upregulation of translational machinery genes. Ribosomal protein genes comprised 30% of upregulated genes, and ~25% of core genome reads mapped to r-proteins during infection versus only 7% in vitro. This pattern was observed in both human patients and mouse infection models, but not in LB cultures despite faster growth.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a major concern that 'the growth rate is deduced from the number of sequencing reads that map to genes for ribosomal proteins' and notes this 'does not necessarily mean that the same applies in vivo.' Reviewer 2 requests additional in vivo validation (CFU counts over time) and notes that other growth-related genes (DNA replication, cell division) are not differentially expressed, which 'would speak against their hypothesis.'

result: UPEC during infection show downregulation of metabolic pathways including amino acid biosynthesis and sugar metabolism, with a switch from sugar transporters to amino acid transporters. The proportion of reads for catabolic genes decreased from 20% in vitro to 11% in patients, and amino acid biosynthesis from 5% to 1%.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes this as part of the 'important discovery that reprogramming occurs, and results in the allocation of cellular resources.' Reviewer 2 describes this as 'reduced expression of metabolic genes in the in vivo isolates compared to the in vitro cultures.' No substantive concerns were raised about these metabolic findings.

result: The authors propose that resource reallocation from metabolic gene expression to translational machinery drives rapid UPEC growth during infection, representing an in vivo manifestation of the bacterial 'growth law' where RNA polymerase is reallocated from metabolic genes to rRNA and ribosomal protein synthesis.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'the study lacks enough data to support this hypothesis' and notes 'this does not necessarily mean that the same applies in vivo.' The mechanistic interpretation linking r-protein expression to growth rate is questioned, with Reviewer 2 requesting additional validation such as CFU counts over time in the mouse model.

result: Exponential growth in rich medium (LB, doubling time ~33 min) cannot recapitulate the infection transcriptional signature, despite faster growth than in urine (54 min). The resource reallocation pattern is infection-specific, as LB-grown bacteria showed intermediate r-protein expression between urine and infection conditions.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the 'comparison of this to growth in vitro and growth in the mouse model of UTI' as a major strength. Reviewer 3 describes the HM43 validation experiments as 'important' and notes they tested 'the effect of a faster growth rate per se.' No concerns were raised about these control experiments.

result: Regulon analysis identified 22 transcriptional factors with differential expression between infection and in vitro conditions, with 18/22 more highly expressed in vitro. These regulons (including Crp, NarL, ModE, MetJ, GadE, YdeO) accounted for 50% of downregulated genes, suggesting multiple environmental cues drive metabolic gene suppression and resource reallocation during infection.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 has 'no substantive concerns regarding the data or major conclusions.' The regulon analysis is presented as supporting evidence for the resource reallocation model. No reviewer specifically challenged the regulon findings or their interpretation.

result: The 14 clinical UPEC isolates showed high genetic diversity (3 phylogroups, 13 sequence types, 13 serogroups), with the majority (10/14) belonging to B2 phylogroup. B1 strains carried fewer virulence factors than B2 strains, yet both established UTIs. Phylogroups showed some differential gene expression but this had a small effect compared to the conserved infection program.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes this work continues efforts 'to define a UPEC virulence genotype during human UTI' and the genetic diversity is part of demonstrating the 'conserved transcriptional signature.' No concerns were raised about the strain characterization or diversity analysis.

result: Expression of virulence factors (iron acquisition, fimbriae, flagella) showed high strain-to-strain variability. Iron acquisition genes were expressed in both conditions but with variable levels. Most samples showed high fim expression (9/14) and low flg expression (12/14), though patient HM07 showed high expression of both.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 acknowledges the work characterizes 'a transcriptional program shared by a genetically diverse group of 14 UPEC strains' and notes the variability in virulence factors. Reviewer 3 notes the study examined 'virulence genes/accessory genes' separately from core genes. No concerns were raised about these observations.

result: Treatment with MICROBEnrich kit does not affect measured bacterial gene expression, as validated by RT-PCR testing with two clinical UTI strains (HM86 and HM56) comparing treated versus untreated samples.
evaluation: This addresses a critical concern from the first review round. In the second round, reviewers request clarification about gene selection for this validation and specifically ask whether r-protein-encoding mRNAs were tested 'given their importance in the study.' The validation data are accepted but reviewers want confirmation about which genes were tested.

result: Approximately 50% of total reads mapped to the core genome regardless of whether bacteria were isolated from patients or cultured in vitro, indicating consistent allocation of transcriptional resources to core metabolic and replication machinery.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes this as part of the finding that 'reprogramming occurs, and results in the allocation of cellular resources to support rapid growth.' No reviewer challenged this observation about the consistent proportion of core genome expression.

result: 492 genes were differentially expressed between infection and in vitro conditions (log2 FC > 2, adjusted p < 0.05), with the majority (343/492) downregulated in patients. Patient samples expressed 94% of core genome versus 99% in vitro, with a higher proportion of genes at low expression levels.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'no substantive concerns regarding the data or major conclusions.' Reviewer 3 describes the differential expression analysis as part of the 'primary result' of the study. No concerns were raised about the statistical analysis or differential expression findings.

result: Analysis of a previously published dataset (Subashchandrabose et al., 2014) showed consistent trends of increased r-protein and decreased catabolic enzyme expression during human UTI. The findings are consistent across multiple studies and patient cohorts, with patients harboring actively dividing bacteria in a specific metabolic state.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 initially asked 'Why didn't the authors include published datasets in their analysis?' The reanalysis was performed and shows consistency. Reviewer 3 notes that Bielecki et al. (2014) 'performed RNAseq on 21 strains from human UTI patients' with similar observations, strengthening the overall result.

result: There was no relationship between patients' previous UTI history and bacterial genotype or gene expression. Patient history of UTI had no effect on bacterial gene expression patterns.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 has 'no substantive concerns regarding the data.' This observation is presented as a negative finding that helps characterize what factors do not influence the conserved transcriptional program. No reviewer challenged this analysis.

result: A core genome of 2653 genes present in all 14 UPEC strains and E. coli MG1655 was identified. High correlation of gene expression was observed between isolates cultured in vitro for both core and accessory genomes. The core genome is enriched for metabolic genes.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes the 'conserved transcriptional signature of the core genome during human UTI' as a major strength. Reviewer 3 describes how 'the analysis was split early between virulence genes/accessory genes and core genes.' No concerns were raised about the core genome definition or analysis approach.

result: All studies including the current one used bacterial RNA isolated from patient urine that was immediately stabilized upon collection. The authors acknowledge they cannot exclude the possibility that gene expression of UPEC in the bladder may differ from UPEC in patient urine.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'take care to attempt to minimize the time between urine sample collection and RNAProtect addition (to be applauded).' The limitation is acknowledged by the authors. Reviewer 1 notes the work provides 'new insight into UPEC adaptation to the human urinary tract' despite this limitation.
